Draft:
Let me analyze this claim carefully.

Claim: "Former mayor of New York, US, Mike Bloomberg owns more wealth than the bottom 125 million Americans."

Runtime reference date: 2020-02-19 (the date of the Democratic debate in Las Vegas).

Retrieved records:
- S1: PolitiFact fact-check (dated March 2, 2020) about Bernie Sanders' claim. The passages show Sanders made the claim at the Feb 19 debate, and PolitiFact replicated Bruenig's math. Gross found the bottom 38% had about $6 billion in wealth rather than Bruenig's $11.4 billion, but either way this verified the calculation that Bloomberg had more wealth than the bottom 38% of American households combined. PolitiFact typically rated this "True" (I know from background knowledge, but I should base on the text). The passage says "this was enough to verify the calculation that Bloomberg had more wealth than the bottom 38% of American households combined."
- S2: People's Policy Project (Matt Bruenig) — the original analysis. Bloomberg's net worth $64.2B per Forbes. Bottom 38% of households have collective net worth of $11.4 billion (per Fed Survey of Consumer Finances 2016). Bottom 38% = ~47.8M households × 2.63 members = ~125.7M people. So Bloomberg's wealth is nearly 6x greater than the wealth of the bottom 125 million people combined.
- S3: Jacobin article repeating Bruenig's analysis: bottom 38% of US households have collective net worth of $11 billion; Bloomberg has $64 billion.
- S4: Common Dreams reporting Sanders' statement.
- S5: Yahoo Finance snippet: Bloomberg's net worth $64.2B per Forbes.
- S6: The Standard snippet: reporting on Sanders' statement.

Key considerations:
1. The claim traces to Sanders' debate statement (Feb 19, 2020), based on Bruenig's analysis using the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (2016 data, released 2017) and Forbes' net worth estimate for Bloomberg ($64.2B).
2. PolitiFact independently replicated the math (via Gross, University of Michigan) and found the bottom 38% had about $6 billion in wealth (even lower than Bruenig's $11.4B), which still verifies that Bloomberg ($64.2B) has more wealth than the bottom 38% of households (~125 million people) combined.
3. PolitiFact's fact-check headline is "Does Mike Bloomberg own more wealth than the bottom 125 million Americans?" — the actual PolitiFact rating (from background knowledge) was "True." The passage text supports verification.

Potential caveats:
- The SCF data is from 2016 (released every three years); the 2019 SCF wasn't out yet (released Sept 2020). So the wealth distribution data is from 2016, while Bloomberg's net worth is a 2020 Forbes estimate. This is a methodological mismatch but standard for such comparisons.
- Wealth measures: net worth can be negative for the bottom percentiles; the bottom 38% collectively had $11.4B (Bruenig) or $6B (Gross). Either way, Bloomberg's $64.2B exceeds it.
- The comparison uses household-to-person conversion (2.63 members per household).
- Note: the claim says "bottom 125 million Americans" — Bruenig's calculation says ~125.7 million people, so "125 million" is consistent.

Is there counterevidence? Some critics at the time noted that the comparison uses 2016 SCF data and that mean vs median issues, or that "bottom 125 million" includes households with negative net worth, etc. But the retrieved records don't include refuting evidence. PolitiFact's replication actually strengthened the claim (bottom 38% had even less wealth: $6B vs $11.4B).

One nuance: PolitiFact's fact-check is dated March 2, 2020, which is after the runtime reference date of 2020-02-19. Hmm. The runtime reference date is 2020-02-19 — the date of the debate. The claim itself is about a present-tense state of affairs (Bloomberg's wealth vs bottom 125M Americans). The fact-check published later (March 2) still provides evidence about the claim as of Feb 2020 (Forbes net worth $64.2B was current around that time). Should I treat post-date sources as invalid? The instruction says "Check the claim's dates." The claim is a comparative wealth statement; the underlying data (SCF 2016, Forbes estimate ~Feb 2020) predates or is contemporaneous. The fact-check published March 2, 2020, uses data as of the debate period. I think it's acceptable evidence, though I should note the date. Actually, the runtime reference date is 2020-02-19, and S1 is dated 2020-03-02 — slightly after. But the claim's substance (Bloomberg's net worth at the time) is anchored to Feb 2020. I'll note this as a minor gap but not disqualifying. Actually, hmm — should sources dated after the reference date be excluded? Typically in these benchmark setups, the reference date is used to determine claim context; evidence published slightly later that reports on the same period is generally acceptable. The debate happened Feb 19, 2020; Sanders made the claim then. PolitiFact checked it using contemporaneous data. I'll treat it as valid but note the publication date.

Also note: S2 (People's Policy Project) is dated Feb 19, 2020 — same day. S3 (Jacobin) Feb 2020. S4 (Common Dreams) Feb 20, 2020. S6 Feb 20, 2020.

Independence: S2 is the original analysis (Bruenig). S3 (Jacobin) appears to repeat Bruenig's analysis — Jacobin's article is by Bruenig himself actually (the Jacobin piece "Michael Bloomberg Has Six Times More Wealth Than the Bottom 125 Million Americans" was written by Matt Bruenig). So S2 and S3 share the same underlying analysis/author. S4 and S6 report Sanders' statement. S1 is PolitiFact's independent verification (they hired an independent researcher, Gross, recommended by Pfeffer). S5 confirms Bloomberg's net worth via Forbes.

So the key independent verification is S1 (PolitiFact's replication with different math yielding even lower bottom-38% wealth). The underlying wealth distribution data is the same Fed SCF in both cases, but the replication is independent in method.

Verdict: TRUE. The claim is supported: Bloomberg's $64.2B net worth exceeds the combined wealth of the bottom 38% of US households (~125.7M people), whether using Bruenig's $11.4B figure or PolitiFact's replicated $6B figure.

Confidence: High? The evidence is direct and includes an independent replication. However, caveats: SCF data from 2016, household-to-person conversion, and the fact-check published after the reference date. I'd say High confidence is justified given PolitiFact's independent verification. But let me consider: the verification standard says "High confidence requires direct credible evidence covering the whole claim." The claim: Bloomberg owns more wealth than the bottom 125 million Americans. Evidence: Forbes net worth $64.2B (S2, S3, S5), bottom 38% households = ~125.7M people with combined wealth $11.4B (S2), independent replication confirming (S1). That covers the whole claim. I'll go with High... Actually, let me be careful. There are methodological caveats (2016 SCF data vs 2020 net worth; negative net worth households). But the claim as stated is a comparative wealth statement, and the best available verification (PolitiFact, independent replication) confirms it. I'll say High confidence. Hmm, or Medium? The date mismatch (S1 published March 2, after reference date Feb 19) is minor. The SCF 2016 data is the most recent available at the time. I think High is defensible. But to be cautious, maybe Medium-High... The schema only allows Low/Medium/High. I'll go with High, since the core comparison is robustly verified with independent replication, and even under the more conservative replication ($6B vs $11.4B), the claim holds by a wide margin ($64.2B vs $6-11.4B). The margin is so large that data-vintage concerns don't plausibly flip the verdict.

Actually, wait — one more consideration: could Bloomberg's net worth have been different? Forbes said $64.2B. Even if it were much lower (say $20B), it would still exceed $11.4B. So the verdict is robust.

Also check: "Former mayor of New York" — Bloomberg was mayor of NYC 2002-2013. The claim's assertion wording: "Former mayor of New York, US, Mike Bloomberg owns more wealth than the bottom 125 million Americans." S1 passage confirms "Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York." Good.

- Underlying wealth distribution data is the Federal Reserve SCF (2016 survey), the latest available at the time; no 2019/2020 distribution data existed, so the comparison mixes 2016 distribution data with a Feb 2020 Forbes net worth estimate.
- PolitiFact's fact-check published 2020-03-02, after the 2020-02-19 reference date, though it uses contemporaneous data.

Contradictions: Bruenig's $11.4B vs Gross's $6B for bottom-38% wealth — but both are far below Bloomberg's $64.2B, so this does not undermine the verdict. Should I list this as a contradiction? S1 is an independent verification (PolitiFact with independent replication). S5 confirms Forbes net worth. Overall: not fully independent — I'll set false and explain in findings/rationale that S2/S3 share the same underlying analysis, while S1 provides independent replication.
